title: The Knots and the Fire: a Mestizo Jesuit, the Lost Historia Occidentalis, and a Man Who Is Made to Die Twice
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Levanto, born in the cloud forest above the Utcubamba
stops.date_confidence: contested year: English Wikipedia gives 1544 or 1545, Spanish Wikipedia gives 1545; month and day are not recorded and default to January 1
stops.campa: A son is born at Levanto, in the ridge country above the Utcubamba, to the Spanish captain Luis Valera, a veteran of the conquest, and an Andean woman the record calls Francisca Perez. He belongs to the first generation born after Francisco Pizarro, children of two peoples who met twelve years earlier at Cajamarca. Quechua and Spanish are both his mother tongues and neither is entirely his. The order he will spend his life inside has not yet decided whether a man of his birth may be permitted to say Mass.
suggested_refs: The district of Levanto, ten kilometers south of Chachapoyas city, where the parish record of the birth has not been located
sources: Sabine Hyland, The Jesuit and the Incas (2003), as cited in the above

stops.name: Chachapoyas, the question of the mother's blood
stops.date_confidence: no date of its own: the lineage claim is tradition attached to the birth year, and the two versions of it are not dated at all
stops.campa: Two traditions claim his mother and they do not agree. One makes Francisca Perez a noblewoman of the court of Atahualpa, which would put Inca royal blood in a Jesuit's veins. The other makes her the daughter of a Chachapoyas curaca, of the people Cusco conquered and who then fought beside the Spanish against Cusco. Both are used to explain the same thing: how a mission priest came to read knotted cord and to argue in Latin that the Incas had law. The atlas records both traditions and merges neither.
suggested_refs: The Chachapoyas curaca lineages absorbed into the Inca state in the 1470s and in revolt against it by 1532
sources: Hyland (2003), citing Chachapoyas oral tradition and Peru province correspondence

stops.name: Trujillo, Latin before the sea
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of both place and year: no document names Trujillo, which Hyland infers from the standard training pattern for mestizo boys; the decade is approximate
stops.campa: The boy is sent down out of the mountains to the coast, to a school at Trujillo where the language of instruction is Latin and the language of correction is Spanish. He learns to parse Cicero in a town founded twenty years before by men who came with his father. The Quechua he speaks at home has no grammar book yet; he will write one of the first. Nothing in the record names the school or the year, and the whole of this schooling is inferred backward from what he is later able to do with three languages at once.
suggested_refs: The colonial schools of Trujillo in the 1550s, none of which preserves an enrollment naming Valera

stops.name: Lima, the course in Arts
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the sources place the Arts course at Lima before the 1568 novitiate but give no year for it
stops.campa: He comes to the City of Kings for the Arts course, logic and rhetoric and natural philosophy, in a capital thirty years old and already the administrative brain of a viceroyalty that runs from Quito to Potosi. The Society of Jesus reaches Peru in 1568 and arrives arguing with itself over who may be admitted to it. Valera is the case the argument is about. He speaks the tongue of the conquered and was baptized in the church of the conquerors, and the mission in the mountains needs a man who can do both without an interpreter.
suggested_refs: The Arts curriculum at Lima in the 1560s, before the founding of the Colegio de San Pablo's full course

segments.name: The Society of Jesus in Peru

stops.name: Colegio de San Pablo, Lima, the novice admitted
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day are not given by any source consulted
stops.campa: Valera enters the Society of Jesus at Lima, among the first mestizos accepted anywhere in Peru for training to the priesthood, at the exact moment when the province cannot agree whether men of mixed parentage should be admitted at all. Three years later, in Rome, Matteo Ricci enters the same novitiate discipline and is set on the road to Ming China. The order is sending both men into sign systems it does not read, with the same instruction: learn the local writing, and prove it was waiting for Christ.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit Peru province catalogs (Litterae Annuae) for the entry class of 1568

stops.name: Huarochiri, sent out for his Quechua
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of pin and year: the assignment to the Huarochiri region is attested, but no source gives a station, a date, or a duration, and the pin takes the modern town
stops.campa: The novice is sent up into Huarochiri, the high province behind Lima where the huacas are still fed and the old shrines still keep their servants, because he can preach without an interpreter. This is what his birth is worth to the order: he is the instrument that reaches where Castilian cannot. He hears the local histories in the language they were composed in. Forty years later another Jesuit campaign in these same valleys will burn the idols and write down the myths, and the manuscript that results will outlive every church built over them.
suggested_refs: The Huarochiri manuscript, compiled in Quechua in the same province a generation later

stops.name: Cusco, ordained by Bishop Lartaun
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given. One lens of the research pool placed the ordination at Lima, which the Spanish-language source contradicts by naming Cusco and the ordaining bishop
stops.campa: After roughly five years as a novice he is ordained priest in the old Inca capital by Bishop Sebastian de Lartaun. He is a mestizo raising the host in the city his father's generation sacked, forty years after Francisco Pizarro rode into it. The Inca nobility of Cusco, dispossessed but not dispersed, take to him at once, and the order notes that they have. Both facts, the ordination and the nobles' favor, will be read against him inside the Society within ten years.
stops.quote: They never made war without causes which appeared to them to be sufficient.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, on Inca conquest practice, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XII, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The episcopate of Sebastian de Lartaun at Cusco, 1573-1583
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Blas Valera' (names the ordaining bishop)

stops.name: Iglesia de la Compania, Cusco, Latin in the old capital
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the Cusco ministry spans the later 1570s and the early 1580s and no single year is fixed for the teaching post
stops.campa: He teaches Latin on the Plaza de Armas, in a Jesuit church raised on the palace of Huayna Capac, and preaches in Quechua to the people who remember whose stones these are. In the same decades and the same viceroyalty Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala is beginning the drawings of quipucamayocs reading their cords to Inca officials. Valera is doing in Latin prose what Guaman Poma will do in Spanish and pen: writing down the administration of a state the Crown insists was a tyranny without law.
stops.quote: The Indians of Peru began to have some kind of government from the time of Ynca Manco Ccapac, and of the King Ynca Rocca, who was another of their Kings.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de la Compania de Jesus on the Cusco Plaza de Armas, built over the Amarucancha
sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)
Anello Oliva, Historia del reino y provincias del Peru (comp. 1631; first publ. 1857/1895)

stops.name: Cusco, the confraternity of the Name of Jesus
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month and day not given
stops.campa: Valera joins the confraternity of the Name of Jesus alongside Inca nobles, kneeling in the same sodality as the grandsons of men who ruled Tawantinsuyu. The Andean aristocracy enters the church here as a Christian gentry in the making and not as a defeated superstition to be broken. In the Latin he is writing at the same time he puts the case plainly: their fathers' religion prepared the ground rather than fouling it. That sentence is the one the Society will punish him for.
suggested_refs: The confraternity registers of the Name of Jesus at Cusco, listing Inca nobles alongside Jesuit priests

stops.name: Cusco, the nobles refuse the transfer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: English Wikipedia dates the attempted transfer and the protest to 1577, while Spanish Wikipedia has him arriving at Juli in the same year; the two postings are not reconciled by either source
stops.campa: The Society moves to send him south to Potosi, and the Inca nobles of Cusco protest the transfer to his superiors. A congregation is telling an order which of its priests it will keep. The protest fails. It is also written down, and what is written down about him at Cusco is read again in Lima ten years later. His parishioners are the old aristocracy. He will not preach that their ancestors were merely devils. A mestizo priest with a following of that kind is a problem the order files and keeps.
stops.quote: The chief was restored to his ancient dignity and lordship.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, on Inca treatment of conquered chiefs, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XII, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: Jesuit province correspondence on the 1577 transfer and the objection from Cusco

stops.name: Juli, the Aymara mission on Titicaca
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1577 by Spanish Wikipedia, which does not hedge it; the year conflicts with the English-language account that has him being pushed toward Potosi at the same date
stops.campa: He goes instead, or also, to Juli on the western shore of Lake Titicaca, the Jesuit mission where the language of the church is Aymara and the doctrine is printed rather than preached from memory. Valera now works in three tongues: Latin for the order, Quechua for the Andes he was born into, Aymara for the altiplano he was sent to. The trilingual books the Church is about to print in Lima will need exactly this man, and the same Church will forbid him to teach a language within six years.
stops.quote: The tribute they paid was their service in the office of decurions.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, on the Inca decimal administration, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XIII, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Jesuit reduction of Juli, the order's principal Aymara-language mission

segments.name: The Silver Mountain and the Gathering

stops.name: Potosi, the confraternity under the silver mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested with a disputed year: English Wikipedia places the transfer around 1578 to 1579, Spanish Wikipedia records him at Potosi in 1582; both datings are kept
stops.campa: The contested transfer finally happens and Valera comes to Potosi, the mountain that is paying for Europe's wars, where the mita drives Andean villages underground in shifts and does not always send them back up. He founds a confraternity here. He is writing, in these years, that the Incas granted the mines to the curacas and taxed labor rather than men, and he is writing it in a city where the labor tax has become a death sentence. His Latin describes the Inca arrangement at length and never once names the mita.
stops.quote: The mines of gold and silver, whether old or newly discovered, were granted to the Guracas.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XIV, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Cerro Rico and the Toledan mita, instituted 1573, five years before Valera's arrival

stops.name: Arequipa, the southern circuit
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: later biographical tradition only, with no primary source naming Arequipa and no year fixed anywhere in the 1580s
stops.campa: Tradition puts him preaching at Arequipa in these years, part of the same southern circuit of Jesuit missions working both the Spanish settlers and the Andean communities they hold. No letter of his places him in the city, and no province catalog names the house. The name keeps appearing in the biographies with no document under it. The road ran that way, and in this decade he is covering a thousand miles of altiplano between one silver town and the next, so the atlas keeps the stop and marks it as tradition rather than dropping a city the itinerary needs.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit circuit of the southern Peruvian missions, Cusco to Arequipa to Potosi
sources: Later biographical tradition summarized in Hyland (2003)

stops.name: Potosi, the second record
stops.date_confidence: attested year from Spanish Wikipedia; it is not clear whether this is a second posting or the same one redated by the other source
stops.campa: He is recorded at Potosi again, still carrying out the research into Andean custom and religion that has become the second half of his life's work. The five volumes of his Historia Occidentalis are accumulating in Latin: the government of the Incas, their laws, their armies, their metals. He notes that they had no iron and made war with copper. The Spanish who read him, when any of them do, will read it as antiquarianism. He is building a case that a state existed here.
stops.quote: Copper, which they called anta, served them in place of iron for making warlike arms.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XIV, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The lost five-volume Historia Occidentalis, known only through quotation

stops.name: Lima, the catechism in two tongues
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the translation work and for the ban; the sequence of cause between the two is a scholarly reading, not a documented one
stops.campa: Back in Lima he works at putting the Catholic catechism into Quechua and Aymara, and argues while he does it that Inca religion is compatible with Christianity, that the Andes were prepared rather than damned. In the same year the Jesuits ban mestizo priests. The order has decided that men of his birth are a risk, and his own writings are cited among the reasons. He goes on translating. The books he is helping to make will be printed and used for two centuries after he is silenced.
suggested_refs: The 1582 Jesuit prohibition on the ordination of mestizos in Peru

stops.name: Lima, the Third Council and the trilingual books
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Third Provincial Council of Lima sat from 15 August 1582 to 18 October 1583 under Archbishop Toribio de Mogrovejo, and the pin takes the opening day of the session
stops.campa: The Third Council of Lima sits for fourteen months and produces the first books printed in South America: a catechism, a confesionario, and a sermonario, each in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara in parallel columns. Valera works on the Quechua and Aymara. The Church has just decided that the faith can be carried in Andean speech, and prints it. In the manuscript he is writing at the same time he records that the Andes already had a way of keeping what mattered, and that it was made of cord.
stops.quote: They wrote them down distinctly by means of knots and threads of different colours which they kept for these purposes, and so taught them to their sons and descendants. Thus the laws that were established by their first kings, six hundred years ago, are now as well preserved in the memories of the people as if they had just been promulgated afresh.
stops.quote_source: Blas Valera, quoted in Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Doctrina Christiana y catecismo para instruccion de los indios, Lima 1584, first book printed in South America

stops.name: Lima, arrested by his own order
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month not given; the arresting house is not named by any source consulted
stops.campa: The Jesuits arrest their own priest. The charge written down is fornication. Four years of imprisonment, then six more with his priesthood suspended. Sabine Hyland, reading the order's internal correspondence, argues the charge on paper is not the reason: what Valera is being punished for is the claim that Inca cosmology prepared the Andes for Christ, which in 1583 is a claim with a name, and the name is heresy. The two accounts stand against each other in the sources and neither is withdrawn.
suggested_refs: Jesuit internal correspondence on the Valera case, cited by Hyland at pp. 69-71 and 176-177

stops.name: Lima, Father Lopez sails to argue for his expulsion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Hyland's reading of the Jesuit correspondence; the departure point is not specified by the source, and the Lima pin is the atlas convention rather than a documented port
stops.campa: On the eleventh of April Father Andres Lopez takes ship for Spain carrying a case: that Blas Valera should be dismissed from the Society altogether. The prosecution of a mestizo priest is now a transatlantic matter, argued in a room in Europe by men who have never heard Quechua spoken. Valera cannot answer it. He is in a cell, and the manuscript that would answer it best, five volumes proving the Andes had law, is in the custody of the people prosecuting him.
suggested_refs: The 1583 embassy of Andres Lopez to the Jesuit generalate on the Valera case
sources: Hyland (2003), pp. 69-71, 176-177, as cited in English Wikipedia, 'Blas Valera'

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the rival account of the scandal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: one thread of secondary tradition puts the scandal at Chuquisaca rather than Cusco, and later writers may have conflated separate incidents; the month is nominal
stops.campa: A second tradition moves the whole affair south to Chuquisaca, seat of the audiencia of Charcas, and tells it as a different scandal in a different city. Sources disagree; some of the disagreement is probably two incidents run together by writers working a century later from hearsay. The atlas keeps the second city on the map beside the first. Everything known about these years comes from the order that was punishing him, and the order does not tell it the same way twice.
suggested_refs: The Audiencia de Charcas at Chuquisaca, alternative site of the 1583 proceedings
sources: Conflicting secondary tradition noted in Hyland (2003)

stops.name: Cusco, the reputed house of correction
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of place, not of fact: neither source names any city of imprisonment, and the Cusco house of correction is a later attribution; the pin is provisional and the year nominal within the four-year term
stops.campa: He is set to prayer and menial labor and taken out weekly for what the order calls mortifications, which in this decade and this house means the whip. He is stripped permanently of his priestly duties and of the right to teach languages: the two things he was admitted for. The Latin manuscript stays in the order's custody while he serves. No document consulted says where the cell was. The atlas pins it at Cusco because the tradition does, and marks the pin as a guess.
suggested_refs: Antonio de Egana, Monumenta Peruana, for the Jesuit disciplinary correspondence of the 1580s
sources: Hyland (2003), pp. 69-71, 176-177, as cited in English Wikipedia, 'Blas Valera'

stops.name: Lima, six years without the Mass
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the post-imprisonment restriction at Lima is dated only approximately, to about 1588 through 1590, by the province catalogs as read by Hyland
stops.campa: The four years of prison end and the six years of suspension run on. He is kept in Lima under restriction while superiors argue about what to do with him and settle nothing for two years. He may not celebrate Mass and he may not teach a language. His chronicle is in a cupboard that belongs to the order. Guaman Poma is walking the same viceroyalty in these years, unlicensed and unpaid, compiling a chronicle nobody has asked for, and neither man knows the other is doing it.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit province catalogs of Peru for 1588-1590, listing Valera's status

stops.name: Rome, the file that decides him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the specific Roman correspondence on the Valera case is not published in full, and the year stands for the period in which reports reached the generalate rather than for a dated document
stops.campa: The reports climb the chain of command, rector to provincial to the generalate, and reach Claudio Acquaviva in Rome, who governs the Society from a desk and has never crossed the Atlantic. This is how the order works everywhere: the field writes, Rome decides. Fifty years later Athanasius Kircher will sit in this same city building whole grammars of Egypt and China out of letters posted home by brethren he never met. Acquaviva reads Peru the same way, and orders Valera out of it.
suggested_refs: The Archivum Romanum Societatis Iesu, holding the unpublished correspondence of the Acquaviva generalate

stops.name: Callao, put aboard for Spain
stops.date_confidence: contested year and reconstructed place: Spanish Wikipedia has him leaving in late 1592, English Wikipedia has him still in Peru or newly at Quito as late as 1594, and no source consulted places him at Callao, which is inferred from the standard fleet route
stops.campa: Acquaviva's order takes effect and Valera is shipped out of the continent he was born on, carrying what is left of his manuscripts. He is forty-seven. He has spent twenty-four years in the Society and ten of them under punishment. Sixty years earlier Francisco Pizarro's ships came up this coast the other way. The mestizo the conquest produced is now being removed from its results by the same institution that ordained him, and the removal is entered in the catalogs as a transfer.
suggested_refs: The port of Callao and the annual Armada del Sur to Panama

stops.name: Quito, two years of illness and the one book that survives
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay and for the composition, though the two-year span is approximate and its start conflicts with the 1592 departure given by the other source
stops.campa: Sick, he is put ashore at Quito and stays roughly two years, writing to Acquaviva to plead his case and getting no reversal. In this room he writes an account of the ancient customs of the natives of Peru, a short book on Inca religion by a man forbidden to preach. It is the only complete work of his that will survive to be read, and it survives because it is short and because it never reached Cadiz. Everything long, everything he considered his real work, is on the ship with him going the other way.
suggested_refs: Relacion de las costumbres antiguas de los naturales del Piru, written at Quito 1594-1595

stops.name: Panama, the isthmus crossed by mule
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the crossing follows the standard sixteenth-century fleet route and no personal account of this leg survives; the date is nominal
stops.campa: The passage to Spain runs the way every passage runs: up the Pacific coast, ashore on the isthmus, mule train through the fever country to the Caribbean side, and a wait for the fleet. No letter of his describes it. The route is reconstructed here from the schedule of the treasure fleets, which is the only thing on that route that moved reliably enough to be reconstructed. He travels under discipline, in the fleet's time and not his own, and the fleet is the part of it the archives kept.
suggested_refs: The Camino Real across the Isthmus of Panama, artery of the Tierra Firme fleet
sources: Reconstructed from standard sixteenth-century transatlantic fleet routes

stops.name: Sanlucar de Barrameda, the Indies fleet makes landfall
stops.date_confidence: contested by roughly a year and reconstructed as to route: Spanish Wikipedia has him reaching Seville in 1595, English Wikipedia dates his arrival in Spain to May 1596; the Guadalquivir landfall is the customary pattern, not a documented fact about him
stops.campa: The fleet comes in over the bar of the Guadalquivir and works upriver toward Seville, which is where the Indies arrive in Spain and where the silver is counted. He has crossed an ocean under an order of exile and lands in a country he has never seen, whose language he was taught by men who told him it was better than his mother's. The two sources disagree by a year about when this happens. They agree that he arrives, and that nobody is waiting for him on the quay except the Society.
suggested_refs: The bar of Sanlucar and the Casa de Contratacion registers of arriving fleets

stops.name: Seville, arrival and a second imprisonment
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia to May 1596, against Spanish Wikipedia's 1595; the imprisonment on arrival is reported without a house or a duration
stops.campa: He is imprisoned on arrival. Ten years of punishment in Peru have not closed the case; the order takes him into custody again on the other side of the Atlantic, in the city where the ships and the paperwork of an empire arrive together. Then, within weeks, the sentence softens. He is to be allowed to teach humanities to boys at Cadiz. He may not teach a language, and he may not hear a confession. The two skills he was recruited for remain forbidden to him for life.
suggested_refs: The Colegio de la Compania at Seville, hub of Jesuit personnel moving between the Indies and Europe

segments.name: Cadiz and the Burning of the Historia

stops.name: Cadiz, permitted humanities and nothing else
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Father Cristobal Mendez reports to Acquaviva on 3 June 1596 that Valera has reformed, and the teaching permission follows
stops.campa: Father Cristobal Mendez writes to Rome on the third of June that Valera has reformed, and Valera is given a classroom in Cadiz: Latin grammar, to Spanish boys, on the Atlantic edge of Andalusia. He is fifty-one years old, has been a priest for twenty-three years and forbidden to act as one for thirteen, and teaches Cicero to children who will never see the Andes. The manuscript of the Historia Occidentalis is in the house with him. He has twenty-seven days left with it.
stops.quote: Father Bias Valera, who wrote a history of that empire in most elegant Latin.
stops.quote_source: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book I ch. VI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Jesuit college at Cadiz and the Mendez report of 3 June 1596
sources: Hyland (2003), pp. 69-71, 176-177, as cited in English Wikipedia, 'Blas Valera'

stops.name: Cadiz, the fleet of Howard and Essex
stops.date_confidence: attested: Spanish Wikipedia gives 30 June, English Wikipedia confirms the sack without the day; the raid ran from 30 June to 15 July 1596
stops.campa: An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Charles Howard and the Earl of Essex takes Cadiz and burns it. Valera is injured. The five volumes of the Historia Occidentalis, the Latin history of the Incas he has been writing for twenty years, go into the fire with the rest of the city's paper. More than half is destroyed outright. A chronicle written to prove that a state existed in the Andes is destroyed in a European raid on a Spanish port, by men who have never heard of the Andes and are there for the silver.
stops.quote: It was the misfortune of my native country...that his papers were lost in the ruin and pillage of Cadiz by the English in 1596. He himself died soon afterwards.
stops.quote_source: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book I ch. VI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The Capture of Cadiz, 30 June to 15 July 1596, under Charles Howard, 1st Earl of Nottingham, and Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Francis Drake' (dead since January 1596 and not present)

stops.name: Seville, the college after the fire
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Hyland places him in likely Jesuit institutional care in his last months, and the Seville attachment is inconsistently reported across secondary biographies; the month is nominal
stops.campa: Some accounts have the injured man carried inland to the Jesuit college at Seville for his last months, in the house through which every letter between Rome and the Indies passes. He has nothing to send through it. What he had is ash at Cadiz, except for the fragments a fellow Jesuit is quietly gathering out of the wreckage, whose existence Valera may never learn of. The order that punished him for twenty years now keeps him, injured, at its own expense.
suggested_refs: The Colegio de la Compania at Seville in the aftermath of the 1596 raid
sources: Hyland (2003), reconstructing likely Jesuit institutional placement

stops.name: Malaga, the last transfer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Malaga stop, reached by way of Jerez de la Frontera in the Spanish-language tradition, is inconsistently reported across secondary biographies and undated within 1596-1597
stops.campa: The Spanish tradition brings him east along the coast, by way of Jerez de la Frontera, to the Jesuit college at Malaga. It is the fourth country he has lived in and his last, and he has been in it for less than two years. He is fifty-two. He has not been permitted to act as a priest since he was thirty-eight. He carries wounds from a raid he had no part in, and he teaches Latin grammar on the far side of an ocean from the country his burned history was about. The secondary biographies report this stop inconsistently.
suggested_refs: The Jesuit college of Malaga, terminus of the Andalusian years
sources: Secondary biographical tradition summarized in Hyland (2003)

stops.name: Malaga, the death with no grave
stops.date_confidence: date attested by both sources, place contested: Spanish Wikipedia names Malaga, English Wikipedia names no city at all and gives only Spain; the pin follows the Spanish-language source and the contradiction is not resolved
stops.campa: He dies on the second of April, about fifty-two years old, of injuries the Spanish source traces back to the sack nine months earlier. Where he dies is disputed. The Spanish record names Malaga; the English-language record names no city at all and says only Spain. No burial entry has been located in either place. The Society of Jesus, which admitted him, ordained him, imprisoned him, suspended him, exiled him and finally housed him, buries him without a monument that anyone since has been able to find.
suggested_refs: The unlocated burial record of Blas Valera, April 1597

stops.name: Cordoba, the papers reach Garcilaso
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Garcilaso in his own first person; the month is not given
stops.campa: Three years after the death, Father Pedro Maldonado de Saavedra puts the rescued fragments into the hands of Inca Garcilaso de la Vega at Cordoba. Garcilaso is another mestizo and another exile, son of a conquistador and a Cusco princess, and he is sitting in Andalusia writing the history of a country he left at twenty-one. More than half of Valera is missing. What is left passes from one half-Inca writer to another in a Spanish town, and no other copy of it exists anywhere.
stops.quote: I received the fragments of papers which were rescued from the pillage, and they caused me regret and sorrow at the loss of those which were destroyed. More than half were lost. I was presented with these papers by the Father Maldonado de Saavedra, a native of Seville, of the same Company, who in the present year 1600 reads the Scripture in the city of Cordova.
stops.quote_source: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book I ch. VI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: Garcilaso's house at Cordoba, where the Comentarios Reales were composed
sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609), Book I ch. VI

stops.name: Lisbon, the Comentarios Reales printed
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the first edition; the month of publication is not recorded here
stops.campa: The first part of the Comentarios Reales de los Incas is printed at Lisbon, and inside it, quoted at length and named, is Blas Valera. Garcilaso says outright that he is translating literally from Valera's Latin and leaning on his authority. This is the form in which the Historia Occidentalis survives: as long quotations inside another man's book, in a third language, chosen by an editor with his own argument to make. The original five volumes are never seen again by anybody.
stops.quote: Father Bias Valera says what follows touching the government of the Yncas, which I have translated literally from his most elegant Latin, because it corroborates what I have already said, and because of the great value of his authority.
stops.quote_source: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Book V ch. XI, trans. Clements R. Markham (Hakluyt Society)
suggested_refs: The 1609 Lisbon first edition of the Comentarios Reales de los Incas
sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)

stops.name: Lima, the Relacion printed at last
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the Loayza edition; the attribution of the Relacion to Valera is itself noted as disputed by the Spanish-language source
stops.campa: Three and a half centuries after it was written at Quito, the account of the ancient customs of the natives of Peru is compiled and published at Lima by the historian Francisco A. Loayza. It is the only Valera a reader can hold entire. Whether it is Valera at all is disputed in the same breath by the same sources that print it. The one complete book bearing his name comes into print in his own country in the same decade that Peruvian scholarship begins arguing about whether he wrote it.
suggested_refs: Francisco A. Loayza, ed., Las costumbres antiguas del Peru y la historia de los Incas (Lima, 1945)

stops.name: Rome, the archives read against the legend
stops.date_confidence: attested publication year of The Jesuit and the Incas; the pin stands for the Jesuit archives the reconstruction rests on rather than for a place Hyland is recorded at
stops.campa: Sabine Hyland publishes The Jesuit and the Incas, rebuilding the documented life out of the order's own catalogs and correspondence: the entry class, the ordination, the charge, the mortifications, the shipping order. Eight years later she publishes an edition and translation of the surviving Relacion, the only text of his a reader can hold entire. The order forbade him to teach a language and kept the file that says so, and four centuries later the file is what puts him back into print.
suggested_refs: Sabine Hyland, The Jesuit and the Incas (2003) and Gods of the Andes (2011)

stops.name: Naples, San Domenico Maggiore, the house the story comes out of
stops.date_confidence: nominal date and reconstructed relevance: the pin marks the Neapolitan clerical world in which the disputed documents are set and dated, not any place Valera is recorded at
stops.campa: Naples, and one convent in it. Giordano Bruno was formed at San Domenico Maggiore and fled a heresy trial out of it in 1576; he is burned at Rome in 1600. Tommaso Campanella lodges in the same house and is tried and jailed in the Neapolitan fortresses from 1591 into the 1620s. Giambattista Vico is schooled by Jesuits a few streets away a century later. Four hundred years after Valera's death, the papers that say he did not die are found in a private archive in this city.
suggested_refs: The convent of San Domenico Maggiore, Naples, and the Neapolitan heresy trials of the 1590s

stops.name: Cusco, the second life claimed
stops.date_confidence: disputed in its entirety: the claim is carried only by the Miccinelli documents, is rejected as fabrication by Rolena Adorno, Juan Carlos Estenssoro and Alfredo Alberdi Vallejo, and has no date of its own beyond following the official 1597 death
stops.campa: The Naples papers tell it differently. In their account the death at Malaga is staged, arranged with the help of the Jesuit Giovanni Anello Oliva, and Valera crosses back to Peru under another name to go on working on Andean writing. Mainstream historiography does not accept a word of it. The atlas pins it anyway, at Cusco, because a claim this specific about a man this thoroughly silenced is part of what happened to him, whether or not it is what happened.
suggested_refs: Exsul Immeritus Blas Valera Populo Suo, published from the Miccinelli archive by Laura Laurencich-Minelli
sources: Laurencich-Minelli, publications on the Miccinelli documents

stops.name: Cusco, the book said to be his
stops.date_confidence: disputed: proponents date the claimed collaboration to about 1600-1615 and Guaman Poma finishes his chronicle in 1615, but the dedicated English Wikipedia article on Guaman Poma contains no discussion of the theory
stops.campa: The same papers claim that the surviving Valera, under a Peruvian identity, wrote or ghost-wrote the Nueva coronica y buen gobierno of Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala. It is a claim that takes the one Andean book that got through and hands it to a Spaniard's son. Guaman Poma specialists reject it. What both men actually left, and what nobody disputes, is a record that the Incas kept their accounts and their law in knotted cord, and that the cords were burned.
suggested_refs: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Nueva coronica y buen gobierno, completed 1615, Copenhagen GKS 2232 4to
sources: Rolena Adorno and other Guaman Poma specialists, per Spanish Wikipedia

stops.name: Cusco, the second death
stops.date_confidence: disputed and internally inconsistent in the research pool: the Historia et Rudimenta is said to have been written before 1618, one lens of the pool gave a second death in 1619 and another in 1618, and the whole claim is rejected by mainstream Jesuit historiography
stops.campa: In this telling he dies a second time, in the Cusco region, twenty-one years after the first death is entered in the record. Two deaths, two decades apart, on two continents, for one man. The historians who reject the papers point out that the second one leaves no more trace than the first: no grave at Cusco either. Cecilia Vicuna, four centuries on, will knot wool in galleries and say what the Spanish did to the cords, which is the part of this story nobody disputes.
suggested_refs: Historia et Rudimenta Linguae Piruanorum, attributed to Cumis, Anello Oliva and Valera, and dated by its claims to before 1618

stops.name: Paris, the facsimile and the argument in print
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Rivet facsimile of Guaman Poma; the later print debate over the Miccinelli documents carried at this pin has no single date and runs from the 1990s onward
stops.campa: Paris publishes the first modern facsimile of Guaman Poma's manuscript, which had sat in Copenhagen unread since the seventeenth century with no shipping record to explain how it got there. The Andean chronicle enters European scholarship as a printed object. Decades later much of the dispute over the Naples papers and Valera's claimed second life circulates through the same city's presses. Two manuscripts crossed the ocean by routes nobody documented, and Paris is where both arguments are held.
suggested_refs: Paul Rivet's 1936 facsimile edition of the Nueva coronica, Institut d'Ethnologie, Paris
sources: Laurencich-Minelli and associated Naples documents scholarship

stops.name: Naples, the papers in the family archive
stops.date_confidence: a range, not a year: the sources date Clara Miccinelli's announcement only to the 1980s and 1990s, with publication by Laura Laurencich-Minelli of the University of Bologna following in the mid-1990s; the pin date is a placeholder inside that range
stops.campa: Clara Miccinelli announces a cache of seventeenth-century papers held privately in Naples: Exsul Immeritus Blas Valera Populo Suo, and Historia et Rudimenta Linguae Piruanorum. They assert that quipus encoded syllables and not merely numbers, that the name of Pacha Kamaq recurs in the knots as phonetic writing, that Pizarro's men poisoned the Incas, and that the priest whose books burned at Cadiz wrote on for twenty-one years after his own funeral.
suggested_refs: The Miccinelli family archive, Naples; the dedicated Wikipedia articles on Exsul Immeritus and the Documentos Miccinelli both returned HTTP 404 in this research session
sources: Laurencich-Minelli, publications on the Miccinelli documents

stops.name: Naples, the papers rejected and half defended
stops.date_confidence: attested for Hyland's published assessment at pp. 227-228; the Peruvian and Italian rebuttals run across the 1990s and 2000s with no single date, and the month here is nominal
stops.campa: Rolena Adorno, Juan Carlos Estenssoro and Alfredo Alberdi Vallejo find the papers apocryphal. Sabine Hyland splits the question: the physical documents are probably genuine seventeenth-century objects, and everything they say is fiction, the anti-colonial argument of some Jesuits of that century dressed as a dead man's testimony. Gary Urton and Bruce Mannheim note how closely the quipu material tracks Raimondo di Sangro's 1751 Lettera Apologetica, which was itself written about the Peruvian knotted cords.
suggested_refs: Raimondo di Sangro, Lettera Apologetica (Naples, 1751), written on the communicative capacity of the quipu
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Blas Valera', citing Hyland 2003, pp. 227-228

stops.name: Chachapoyas, no monument located
stops.date_confidence: not an event: an absence-of-evidence finding as of the sources reachable on this date, and not a claim that no monument exists anywhere
stops.campa: In the region he was born in, no statue, no street, no plaza, no school carries his name in anything reachable. The Spanish Wikipedia article on Chachapoyas does not mention him. There is no marked grave in Spain and no burial entry found in either candidate city. The first mestizo chronicler of Peru, who argued that Quechua could carry the doctrine as well as Latin, is commemorated nowhere the search could reach. This is a gap in the record, stated as a gap.
suggested_refs: Municipal and regional records of Amazonas and Chachapoyas, not reachable with the tools available in this session
sources: Search of Spanish Wikipedia, 'Chachapoyas', which contains no mention of Valera
